initial_presentation: A 32-month-old Egyptian girl was referred to the pediatric endocrinology unit for evaluation of poor growth. She is the second-born female child to consanguineous Egyptian parents, with one normal sibling. She was born at term via normal vaginal delivery in a private hospital and cried immediately at birth. Her birth weight was 1.5 kg and length was 35 cm. At 12 days old, she experienced multifocal seizures, and hypocalcemia was detected. Serum parathormone (PTH) level was not checked due to lack of facilities. The seizures were managed with intravenous calcium infusions. Subsequently, she required calcium and alfacalcidol to maintain calcium levels and has been on calcium and vitamin D supplements since then. At one year old, her weight was 4.800 kg and height was 48 cm. Despite a good appetite, she was not thriving well. There was no history of recurrent infections or previous hospital admissions. On examination, she was found to be severely growth retarded with normal mentality. Her weight was 7 kg, height 60 cm, and head circumference 38 cm (all far below the third percentile). The upper segment to lower ratio was normal. Dysmorphic features included microcephaly, deep-set eyes, peaked nose, thin lips, micrognathia, low set ears, and a depressed nasal bridge. Systemic examination, including the cardiovascular system, was within normal limits. Ophthalmic examination did not reveal any abnormalities.

A 49-year-old male patient presented with a history of low vision following a childhood traffic accident. He underwent laser treatment in both eyes at the age of 12 and again one month prior to the current visit. Additionally, he had bilateral laser-assisted in situ keratomileusis in 2002. His medical and family histories were otherwise unremarkable. He was born full term via normal delivery.

A 32-year-old individual presented for a rheumatologic evaluation due to several months of fatigue, dry eyes, dry mouth, weight loss, hair loss, joint pain, and shortness of breath during physical activity.
A 30-year-old Vietnamese female presented with fatigue, muscle weakness, memory loss, unintentional weight gain, hair loss, and amenorrhea.

A 58-year-old man with a history of coronary artery disease and coronary bypass surgery in 2005 presented with sclerodactyly and digital pitting scars on multiple fingers, along with palmar and facial telangiectasias, and tightness of the lips and skin around the neck. Capillaroscopy showed capillary nailfold dropout. He also had gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Over the years, the sclerodactyly worsened; in 2011, he developed exertional dyspnea and was found to have pulmonary fibrosis. Testing for antinuclear antibodies (ANA) by indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) using Hep2 cells showed a clumpy nucleolar and coilin body staining pattern in interphase cells at a dilution of 1:640, and a 34-kDa band on Western blotting, indicating reactivity to fibrillarin. Tests for rheumatoid factor, antibodies for double-stranded DNA, RNP, Smith, Scl-70, centromere, SS-A, SS-B, Jo-1, and cyclic citrullinated peptide were negative, and serum complement levels were normal. His condition remained stable without immune modulators until 2014 when he developed pulmonary hypertension and was started on hydroxychloroquine. In 2015, he developed photosensitive erythematous lesions on the upper trunk and neck. These lesions were succulent, non-scaly pink elevated plaques on the trunk, resembling a livedo reticularis-like pattern.

A 77-year-old male with a medical history including post-traumatic stress disorder, multiple cerebrovascular accidents, chronic kidney disease stage 3b, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, type 2 diabetes mellitus, diabetic neuropathy, and benign prostatic hyperplasia presented with symptoms of increasing confusion, altered mental status, dystonia, tremor, and hallucinations. The family reported no history of neurological disease. The patient's daughter noted that he exhibited confusion and inappropriate speech. Upon admission for evaluation of altered mental status, the patient was alert and oriented to person, place, time, and situation in the emergency department, though he exhibited shuddering while remaining neurologically intact. The patient displayed aggressive and agitated behavior and began wandering the hallways, necessitating 1:1 observation. A psychiatry consultation was requested for further evaluation.

A 7.5-year-old boy was admitted to the endocrinology clinic with concerns about short stature. He was born at 40 weeks of gestation as the first child of parents who are not related by blood, following a pregnancy that included polyhydramnios. His birth weight was 3500 grams. On physical examination, his height was 103 cm (-4 standard deviations) and his weight was 16 kg (below the 3rd percentile, -1.7 standard deviations). He exhibited distinctive craniofacial features such as curly and dry hair, sparse eyebrows, a coarse facial appearance, a broad nasal tip with upturned nostrils, downslanting palpebral fissures, dysplastic ears, hyperextensible fingers, and unusual skin characteristics including dry, itchy, elastic skin, a hairy nevus on the left thigh, and congenital overlapping toes. An eye examination showed bilateral optic nerve hypoplasia, intermittent strabismus, ptosis, and mild telecanthus.

A 55-year-old male visited the outpatient department with complaints of jaundice for 15 days, a weight loss of approximately 2 kilograms over the same period, and generalized weakness for 15 days. The patient was alert and oriented to time, place, and person. Vital signs included a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation at 98%, blood pressure of 110/70 mmHg, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15. Random blood sugar was measured at 153 mg/dl. The patient reported a history of dark-colored urine. Physical examination revealed pallor, but no signs of icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or edema. The patient denied experiencing abdominal pain, constipation, loose stools, fever, backache, or respiratory symptoms such as cough or breathlessness. The patient had no known history of chronic conditions such as diabetes mellitus, hypertension, tuberculosis, or bronchial asthma, and no significant surgical history. Additionally, the patient was not known to have Hepatitis B or HIV. On palpation, hepatomegaly was noted.

A 17-year-old female, born from a non-consanguineous marriage, visited the dermatology outpatient department with a history of skin and joint laxity. She reported frequent bruising and gaping wounds from minor trauma, but no major hemorrhagic incidents. She was born full-term via normal delivery with no neonatal or perinatal complications. There were no similar complaints in her family history, including parents and siblings. Physical examination revealed soft, velvety, and hyperextensible skin with normal recoil. Atrophic scars resembling cigarette paper were observed on the forehead, cheeks, forearms, elbows, knees, and shins. The joints exhibited hypermobility, genu recurvatum of the knees, and hallux valgus deformity of both great toes. Gorlin's sign and reverse Namaskar sign were present. There was no evidence of ecchymosis, cyanosis, digital clubbing, jaundice, or lymphadenopathy.

An 11-year-old girl with no prior health issues, medications, or allergies experienced complications with the eruption of her left maxillary canine tooth (23) and first premolar (24). Panoramic tomography revealed significant resorption on the mesial side of the root of tooth 24. There was no history of trauma in the affected area. Clinical examination showed marginal gingivitis around teeth 22-24, both labially and buccally, along with external resorption of tooth 24. Gingival pockets measuring 6-8 millimeters in depth were found adjacent to teeth 23 and 24. The patient reported soreness in the area. An orthodontic specialist noted a lack of space, leading to the extraction of tooth 24 and enucleation of granulation tissue. No tissue was collected for further analysis at that time. Twelve weeks later, a significant bone defect was noted, and tooth 23 remained in infraocclusion. The patient was referred to the Department of Oral and Maxillofacial Surgery at Turku University Hospital (TUH) in Turku, Finland. At TUH, the bone defect was confirmed. Clinical examination showed no swelling, deep gingival pockets, or mobility of the teeth in the affected region. Adjacent teeth were vital, though there was a slight decrease in vitality in the second premolar and first molar. The gingiva in the region exhibited a bluish discoloration. Panoramic and intraoral X-rays indicated external resorption in the roots of the left maxillary lateral incisor and canine teeth. An osteolytic area in the same region (teeth 22-23) was consistently observed with an image taken three months earlier. Cone beam tomography revealed a cystic, osteolytic area on the left palatal side of the roots from the lateral incisor to the first premolar. The palatal cortex was perforated.
